source_text: So it occurred to me that "at -40°, water thrown into the air turns into crystals before it hits the ground".  That could be a useful guiding principle for our DB.

That could be a useful guiding principle for our DB.

reply_text:
㊥ ("water thrown into the air turns into crystals before it hits the ground") I like it. As a working rule I'd read it as: structure is added at write time, on the way in, so nothing reaches the store as a raw puddle waiting to be organised later.

🈖 (what that means concretely for -40°)
- **Hot memory is the puddle.** A Claude memory file lands as liquid text. Any structure (versions, conflicts, duplicates, entities) only comes from batch passes run afterwards, which is what we've been doing for two days.
- **Crystallising in flight means the ingest step does that work.** When a memory is written, it gets a dated version, its links, its entities, and a conflict check against the memories it overlaps, all before anyone reads it.
- **The crystal still holds the water.** The exact text is kept byte for byte (the milestone 1 guarantee); the structure is added around it, never substituted for it.
- **Crystals need nuclei.** New text attaches to existing structure: the seed aliases, known entities and the pattern graph. A memory that matches nothing stays visibly unattached, and that's useful to see.

㊢ (where we are against it) The ingest hook already does the first part at write time: exact version and links. Entities and the conflict check still only run as batches.

㊭ (making the hook live up to it)
1. **Synchronous, cheap:** rule-based entity extraction (seed aliases, repos, seats, ports) runs in the hook itself. It's regex work, a few milliseconds.
2. **Shortly after, expensive:** the hook queues the new memory for a Haiku entity pass and for judging against its candidate pairs. A small bg.py worker drains the queue, so within a few minutes a new memory has entities and any conflict is an open sorry. The hook stays fast and never waits on a model.

The same shape would apply to the FUTON debugger idea later: an error crystallises into an open item with its context as it's raised, not when someone gets round to it.

🈸 (go?) Shall I build 1 and 2? I'd also fix the `about` date-ordering issue on the way, since a new memory's place in the timeline is part of what has to be settled at write time.

previous_reply_acts.text: ("Is that clarifying?") Yes, more than I expected. The 3/2 document isn't about search: it's about deciding whether a constructed cascade is structurally sound before anyone scores it. But its pasting operation has the same shape as your accumulator, and that tells me what a cascade search over memories would need.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text:
(why the gaps I sent codex-68 matter here) Two of them are exactly where memory search would hit trouble:
1. **Pasting needs identical objects, but steps from different memories only match up to renaming.** One memory says "Agency", another says ":7070". Joining them needs a gluing iso, plus a lemma that validity survives transport along it, and that lemma doesn't exist yet.
2. **Gluings have no coherence condition.** Paths through several memories could identify things inconsistently, and nothing currently rules that out.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text: (where part 2 fits) The entity aliases I just built are candidate identifications across memories, i.e. raw material for gluings. The doc forbids gluings inferred from coincident names, which matches how I've treated merges so far: proposed, never applied automatically. In this framing the store would offer gluing *candidates*, and admitting one would need authored evidence.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-15
previous_reply_acts.text: (what I can't say yet) This is my reading of the shapes, not a checked correspondence. In particular, I haven't verified that the WM's squares are meant to be read as refinement steps. codex-68 would know whether that reading holds.
